summary:
We are developing an interactive sky exploration platform that uses NASA's SPHEREx data to help users investigate the changing infrared sky. Through a 2D celestial atlas, users can explore regions of the sky, inspect astronomical sources, and compare observations across different epochs.

The platform aims to process observations across available time periods, identify and track sources, and analyze changes in their positions, brightness, and infrared spectra. By cross-referencing potential moving objects with existing astronomical catalogues, it will highlight unusual or unexplained detections as candidates for further investigation. Users can explore these findings through interactive visualizations, source timelines, motion graphs, and spectral information.

Our goal is to make complex astronomical data more accessible while creating a systematic way to investigate potentially overlooked celestial objects. By combining data analysis, visualization, and automated candidate screening, the project seeks to turn large-scale space observations into an accessible tool for exploration and scientific discovery.
details:
Our project is designed as an interactive astronomical investigation platform built around NASA's SPHEREx infrared observations. Its core consists of a data-processing pipeline and a web-based visualization interface.

The processing pipeline retrieves available SPHEREx observational data from NASA's IRSA archive and organizes observations according to their sky coverage, observation times, and available spectral information. Using astronomical image-processing techniques, the system detects individual sources, determines their celestial coordinates, measures their brightness, and extracts their spectral measurements where available.

A major part of the system is cross-epoch analysis. Sources detected in different observations are matched to identify the same astronomical objects across time. Their positional changes, brightness variations, and other measurable differences are then analyzed. Potentially moving or variable sources are investigated further by checking detection reliability and comparing their positions with existing astronomical catalogues. This helps distinguish known objects from unusual detections that may deserve further investigation.

Whole-Sky Processing and Region-Based Exploration

Instead of processing the entire dataset every time a user selects a region, our proposed architecture organizes precomputed source measurements and observational information into a searchable database. This allows the platform to retrieve relevant sources and candidate objects according to the region selected by the user.

The system is intended to support both broad sky exploration and detailed investigation of smaller regions. This approach aims to reduce repeated computation while providing a consistent experience across different viewing scales.

Main Features

1. Interactive Sky Atlas: A two-dimensional celestial map where users can navigate the sky, zoom into regions, select areas, and explore detected astronomical sources.

2. Epoch Comparison: Users can compare available observations of a selected region or individual object across different observation times, examining positional changes and brightness variations.

3. Automated Candidate Scanner: The system identifies potentially moving or variable sources, evaluates their observational evidence, and checks existing catalogues for known-object matches. Unmatched detections are presented as candidates for further investigation rather than automatically classified as discoveries.

4. Object Exploration: Users can select individual sources to inspect their available observational information, including celestial coordinates, brightness, spectral characteristics, and catalogue associations.

5. Timeline and Scientific Visualizations: Interactive graphs and visualizations allow users to examine source positions, motion estimates, flux variations, and infrared spectra across available observations.

Technology and Development Approach

The scientific data-processing component is designed around Python and its astronomical and scientific computing ecosystem. Planned tools include Astropy for astronomical coordinates and FITS data handling, Astroquery for accessing astronomical archives and catalogues, Photutils for source detection and photometry, and NumPy and Pandas for numerical processing and data organization.

The web interface is designed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Aladin Lite for interactive celestial visualization and Chart.js for scientific graphs and data visualization. Processed results will be organized into a format that the frontend can retrieve efficiently.

The development prioritizes publicly accessible astronomical data and free or open-source technologies to keep the platform accessible without requiring expensive computing infrastructure.

Creativity, Benefits, and Intended Impact

The central innovation is the integration of spatial exploration, multi-epoch comparison, spectral investigation, and automated candidate screening into a unified platform. Rather than simply displaying astronomical images or catalogues, the system aims to help users investigate how celestial sources behave across observations and identify unusual patterns that might otherwise require extensive manual inspection.

The platform is intended for both general space enthusiasts and astronomy students or researchers. Beginners can explore the infrared sky through an intuitive visual interface, while more advanced users can investigate observational measurements and scientific graphs.

By making complex astronomical observations easier to navigate, compare, and investigate, our project aims to encourage data-driven exploration and support the identification of potentially overlooked celestial objects.
